svg.text: FIG 07: AC TRANSIENTS, TRANSIENT-FREE SWITCHING & S-DOMAIN EQUIVALENTS
Sinusoidal RL & RC Transients • θ = φ Switching Invariant • Max DC Offset Doubling • Laplace Transform Circuits

g.text: Excitation applied at t = 0: v(t) = V_m · sin(ωt + θ).
KVL loop equation: L · di/dt + R · i = V_m · sin(ωt + θ)
i(t) = I_m · sin(ωt + θ - φ) + A · e^{-t / τ}
• φ = tan⁻¹(ωL / R) = Circuit impedance angle
• τ = L / R = Inductive circuit time constant
Applying boundary condition at t = 0⁺ with unenergized inductor (i(0⁺) = 0):
0 = I_m · sin(θ - φ) + A ==> A = -I_m · sin(θ - φ)
i(t) = I_m · sin(ωt + θ - φ) - [I_m · sin(θ - φ)] · e^{-(R/L)t}
• Steady-State Part: Undamped sinusoid lagging voltage by angle φ.
• Transient Part: Unidirectional DC offset exponential dying at rate R/L.
If DC offset is large, initial peak current can reach up to nearly 2·I_m!
For series RC excited by v(t) = V_m · sin(ωt + θ):
Capacitor steady-state voltage leads/lags by φ_c = tan⁻¹(-1 / (ωRC)):
v_C(t) = V_Cm · sin(ωt + θ - φ_c) + A_c · e^{-t / RC}
i(t) = I_m · cos(ωt + θ - φ_c) + (A_c / R) · e^{-t / RC}
Notice that i(0⁺) jumps discontinuously to [V_m · sin(θ) - 0] / R!
The transient exponential term is A · e^{-t/τ} where A = -I_m · sin(θ - φ).
θ - φ = 0 or ±π ==> θ = φ = tan⁻¹(ωL / R)
Switch must close at the exact instant when the voltage waveform phase
At this instant, steady-state current i_ss(0) is PRECISELY ZERO,
matching the inductor's initial resting state i_L(0⁻) = 0 A!
Result: Pure steady-state sinusoid immediately from t = 0!
To maximize the transient DC offset (Worst Case for circuit breakers!):
Special Case: Pure Inductive Circuit (R → 0, φ = 90°):
• Max transient occurs if θ = 0° (switch closes at voltage zero crossing!).
Peak current reaches i_{max} = 2 · I_m (Doubling DC offset!)
Creates massive electromagnetic stress on transformer windings and breakers!
• For Inductor (prefers current = 0): Close switch when steady-state current = 0.
• For Capacitor (prefers voltage = 0): Close switch when steady-state voltage = 0.
Laplace transform converts time-domain differential equations into algebraic equations.
Initial conditions are absorbed directly as internal independent sources!
Always evaluate initial conditions at t = 0⁻ to capture impulsive transitions cleanly!
Time domain relation: v_L(t) = L · di_L/dt
Laplace transform: V_L(s) = sL · I_L(s) - L · I₀
Impedance sL IN SERIES WITH opposing source L · I₀
Admittance 1/(sL) IN PARALLEL WITH current source I₀ / s
Thévenin voltage source has (+) terminal pointing in direction of initial current I₀!
Time domain relation: i_C(t) = C · dv_C/dt
Laplace transform: I_C(s) = sC · V_C(s) - C · V₀
Impedance 1/(sC) IN SERIES WITH voltage source V₀ / s
Admittance sC IN PARALLEL WITH current source C · V₀
Thévenin voltage source V₀/s has same polarity as initial voltage V₀!
Algorithm to solve any arbitrary transient network via Laplace:
1. Draw t < 0 circuit: Find initial states i_L(0⁻) and v_C(0⁻).
2. Draw s-domain equivalent for t > 0 with initial condition sources.
3. Apply Nodal or Mesh analysis in s-domain to get algebraic X(s).
4. Perform partial fraction expansion on X(s).
5. Invert via ℒ⁻¹ to obtain exact time-domain response x(t)!
Immune to boundary state errors! Handles Dirac impulses δ(t) automatically!
Drill 1: AC Transient-Free Angle Calculation (GATE PYQ)
Circuit: Series RL with R = 10 Ω, L = 0.0318 H (L ≈ 10/π H), f = 50 Hz.
Excitation: v(t) = 230√2 · sin(100π t + θ) V.
Question: Determine switching angle θ for zero transient current.
φ = tan⁻¹(X_L / R) = tan⁻¹(10 / 10) = tan⁻¹(1) = 45° (π / 4 rad)
If switch closes at θ = 45°, current immediately enters steady state I = 23 A RMS!
Drill 2: s-Domain Laplace Solution of Switched RC
Given: Series RC with R = 2 Ω, C = 0.5 F, initial voltage v_C(0⁻) = 4 V.
At t = 0, connected to step source V_s(t) = 10 · u(t) V.
Series initial voltage source = V₀ / s = 4 / s (aiding V_s)
v_C(t) = 10 - 6 · e^{-t} · u(t) V (Matches Universal Formula!)
Drill 3: Initial and Final Value Theorems in s-Domain
Given Laplace transform of output response X(s) = (5s + 20) / [s(s² + 4s + 13)].
Evaluate x(0⁺) and x(∞) WITHOUT inverting the transform!
Poles of s·X(s) are roots of s² + 4s + 13 = 0 → s = -2 ± j3 (strictly in LHP!).
Therefore FVT is 100% VALID! (If poles were on jω-axis or RHP, FVT FAILS!).
